Elongation angles —
We compute the angles from the Sun, the Earth-center and the

P OTENTIAL APPLICATIONS
Although the AbC is meant for astrometry, it can also be used
as an astrometric tool to characterize ADCS and imagers.
Here are examples in both application contexts.
Astrometry to commission ADCS and Imager
The ADCS performance strongly depends on the rest of the
platform, its preferred orientation (OPS-SAT observes mainly
with−Z axis to the Earth, while the ADCS’ star tracker
points perpendicularly to this direction) and the reliability of
space-environment models. It makes it very difﬁcult to test
for acceptance.

Interestingly, our ﬁrst 3-Unit CubeSat at Paris
Observatory, PICSAT, launched in 2018 (Nowak 2018 [12])
used the same ADCS like OPS-SAT (BST iADCS-100), but
provided by Hyperlink Technologies B.V ., Netherlands, with
the star tracker ST200 aligned with the line of sight of the
telescope (+Z axis). In 8 weeks of operations, the ADCS
was never able to align the satellite with the star β−Pictoris,
its primary target, despite the detumbling reached less than
0.1◦/s, well below the manufacturer’s request.

[1] (arxiv-refined-astrometry#c010) The astrometric reduction has mainly remained a task
assigned to the ground segment of the space missions. It
allows extensive algorithms and checks that are obviously
worth being performed on ground, although it requires an
important telecommunication budget.
The next section will present our AbC method in details.
Section 3 reminds ESA’s OPS-SAT mission and our exper-
iment “Id.156” in OPS-SAT. Section 4 presents our possible
application and calls for further use with various contexts and
hardware.
2. A NGLE -BASED ASTROMETRIC REDUCTION
The AbC method is a full process combining linear estimate
optimization and quaternion algebra.

[2] (arxiv-refined-astrometry#c012) Then,
the beacon is assumed to be present within a maximum
parallaxσπ from a pre-computed direction, based on mission
preparation work, that is not discussed here. The imager is
pointed to the pre-computed direction of the beacon and puts
it in a central region of the image, whose half-size is lower
than σπ +σACE, where σACE is the attitude control error of
the platform (including the imager, assumed to be ﬁxed). In
this region of the image, the platform’s ADCS informs about
the estimated pointing with an accuracyσAKE. Typically, with
nowadays CubeSat hardware, one can expect an imager with
a ﬁeld of view FoV∼ 10◦ and an ADCS with σACE∼ 0.1◦
